research.title: Water transport in the Bronze Age of the Russian Plain

prompts.Warship:
Use case: stylized-concept. Create ONE new Russian-culture BRONZE AGE boat master for the historical RTS game Age of Fronts. The reference is an approved earlier Stone Age boat: use ONLY its polished painterly game-art style, wood/material rendering, warm upper-left lighting, orthographic overhead camera and clean transparent asset presentation. This is a new next-age design, not an edit to the reference file.
Straight vertical overhead orthographic view, camera exactly perpendicular to the boat's deck, bow points precisely screen-up, stern screen-down. No perspective, no isometric angle, no visible vertical exterior hull sides. Square RGBA canvas, genuine fully transparent background. One complete centered vessel with immaculate transparent margins. Keep all objects and oar/paddle tips inside the canvas. No cast shadow floating outside the vessel, no water, wake, shoreline, scene, UI, text, crew, or sprite-sheet frames.
Match the crisp semi-realistic painted style of the reference, thick believable timber members, clearly connected joints, hand-adzed grain and restrained large material shapes. This will be viewed at 24-48 pixels: prioritize readable role silhouette and a few large masses rather than tiny decorative clutter. Make a convincing advance in craft and finish from Stone Age while retaining the eastern-European forest/river material language. Regional prehistoric inspiration, not an archaeological reconstruction of a proven specialized vessel class. Timber, birch bark, bast-fibre or rawhide cord, modest bronze weapons/traded metal are appropriate. No modern Russian flags, coats of arms, religious crosses, stars, Soviet emblems, Viking dragon heads, medieval shield bosses, iron nails, iron bands, steel, guns, cannon, Greek trireme decorations, tropical outriggers, fantasy gold ornament. No sails or mast for this river-craft concept.
SUBJECT: Russian Bronze Age WARSHIP. A long, narrow, powerful river fighting boat with one dark warm-brown hollowed oak hull, refined smooth adzed inner walls, substantial continuous carved gunwales, and four pale crosswise rowing benches. Its central hull is about four times longer than wide, overall visible length including bow and stern about 84% of the square canvas height. Four matched PAIRS of broad wooden working oars, one oar per side at each bench (exactly eight oars), extend a modest distance outward and slightly toward stern. Every shaft visibly joins a practical wooden thole peg and loose rawhide retaining loop at the gunwale; no disconnected oars or metal rowlocks. Including oars the silhouette is about 2.4 times longer than wide. Two large leaf-shaped cast BRONZE spearheads, golden-copper metal with bright clean edge highlights, terminate long wooden spare spear shafts secured along the upper gunwales, tips pointing toward bow. Bold paired reddish ochre rawhide gunwale wraps at midships preserve the readable combat accent of the approved earlier boat. A small open bow fighting platform of joined broad timber slats, realistically supported, without ram, canopy or siege engine. Interior otherwise clear and empty, no cargo. No shields. Strong pointed bow and tapered stern, purposeful coordinated oar silhouette and prominent bronze weapon cue. Large crisp forms that survive downscaling, no busy micro-ornament.

SUBJECT: Russian Bronze Age TROOP TRANSPORT. A broad, rounded, framed BIRCH-BARK passenger boat inspired by prehistoric forest-zone river craft. Warm pale ivory birch-bark shell with naturally mottled bark and clearly sewn rawhide/root seams around the rim; substantial brown wooden gunwales and a believable internal timber frame support the shell, with visible ribs at the inner sides. This is a wide single hull, NOT two pontoons. Overall length about 84% of square canvas height and width about 44%, compact rounded outline roughly 1.9 times longer than wide. Six substantial pale honey-wood crosswise passenger benches, evenly spaced across a dark clear open interior, supported by visible wooden brackets/ribs. The bench rows form six large readable horizontal bands. Light hide pads only on the first and last bench, kept visually distinct from cargo. A pair of long leaf-bladed wooden paddles stowed and securely lashed alongside the outer sides, do not dominate the silhouette. Blunt rounded bow and stern, thicker stitched pale bark edges than the Stone Age hollowed log. No weapons, spears, shields, cargo, containers, baskets, pottery, sacks, canopy or roof. The entire open interior is visibly reserved for passengers. Plausible seated weight carried by frame members, no floating benches. Pale broad shell and orderly empty seats must read as transport at a glance.

SUBJECT: Russian Bronze Age TRADE BOAT. A broad, compact twin-log cargo craft with two robust dark-brown hollowed oak pontoons joined by six substantial transverse timber beams and a wide low slatted freight platform. Refined smooth adzed wood and carefully planned recessed lash points give a meaningful construction advance over the Stone Age raft. Overall outer length about 78% of square canvas height and width about 51%, broad rectangular outline roughly 1.5 times longer than wide, centered. Two short blunt rounded bow tips visible at screen-top, not tall spikes. All beams connect physically into the pontoons with convincing bast bindings and supported platform edges. Six large SECURED commercial cargo masses arranged in two orderly columns of three: one broad golden woven basket holding a small stack of dull copper/bronze raw-metal pieces, one large pale hide-wrapped bale, one broad woven grain basket, one reddish unglazed clay jar with a visible dark round mouth, one tan sewn leather goods bundle, and one dark rolled fur bale. Copper pieces are simple irregular cast bars/metal chunks, no modern gold bars or decorative weapons. The large contrasting tan, cream, copper and red cargo masses cover most of the cargo platform and sit firmly on it with thick crossed bast ties. A low bare stern work platform holds two neatly stowed wooden steering paddles with visible retaining cords. No passenger bench rows, weapons, shields, sail, mast or canopy. Redraw exactly FOUR MATCHED PAIRS, eight wooden working oars total, one pair at each of the FOUR rowing benches. Keep their same attachment positions and their outward, stern-angled stroke pose. Each oar must be one clearly CONTINUOUS solid wooden object: a visible inner hand grip extending inward past its rawhide rowlock into the open boat beside its corresponding bench, a long tapered shaft passing through the gunwale/thole attachment, and an entire broad smooth LEAF-SHAPED wooden paddle blade. Show all eight COMPLETE rounded blade ends clearly against transparent space. Preserve matching mirrored pairs, plausible uniform wood thickness and grain continuity from shaft through blade. Leave generous transparent clearance around the oars. Keep the original hull size and framing; all oar tips fit safely inside the 1254x1254 canvas, with no cropping or concealment. The image already has four oar pairs: do not remove or duplicate any.
Everything apart from those eight working oars is invariant: the dark single oak hull, pure vertical overhead orthographic camera, bow precisely screen-up, two golden-bronze spearheads and secured spare spear shafts at the bow, upper slatted bow fighting platform, four crosswise rowing benches, ochre gunwale wraps, stern and bow ties, beautiful polished painterly material textures and warm upper-left lighting. prompts.WarshipStraightOarsV5:
Use case: precise-object-edit.
IMAGE 1 is the edit target: the Russian Bronze Age overhead warship master. Keep its boat, materials, light, framing, canvas size and all non-oar details.
IMAGE 2 is an EXACT WORKING-OAR GEOMETRY AND LAYOUT GUIDE on the same 1254 x 1254 coordinate grid, NOT a style reference. Use its eight straight wooden forms to replace the malformed working oars of Image 1. Render those eight guide shapes in Image 1's beautiful painterly wood style.

DELETE all EIGHT existing bent working oars of Image 1, including their bent inner grips, bulbous elbows and distorted little handle stubs. Replace them with exactly FOUR matched pairs of COMPLETE STRAIGHT RIGID OARS in the positions and orientation of Image 2. Every left-bank oar is parallel to the other left-bank oars; every right-bank oar is parallel to the other right-bank oars. Left and right are mirrored, all sweep outward and toward stern. Exactly eight wooden working oars. The two bronze-tipped spare spears along the bow sides are NOT oars and must remain unchanged.

CRITICAL PHYSICAL RULE: For EACH oar, the center of its visible inner handgrip, the centerline of its shaft, and the long center axis of its paddle blade form ONE PERFECTLY STRAIGHT LINE in this purely overhead view. No kink at the gunwale, no elbow, no curved rod, no bent grips, no offset blades, no hinge, no spherical joint, no foreshortening, no flexible rope shaft. An oar is a single straight stick with a flat blade attached on the same axis. The long continuous brown shafts of Image 2 pass straight across the gunwale and extend into the open boat near each rowing bench; the handles continue along that same straight axis. All eight shafts must obey this, including the two rear pairs that previously had missing internal grips.
The blade contours follow the guide's COMPLETE smooth rounded leaf forms. All eight blades are uncut and complete with safe transparent clearance. Replace the flat guide shading with realistic warm grain, clean edges and restrained painterly highlights, without warping its straight geometry.
Attach each straight shaft to the gunwale with a small separate vertical wooden thole peg beside the shaft and a loose rawhide retaining loop. The thole peg is NOT part of the shaft: it must never introduce a bend or a round ball into the oar itself. The gunwale can occlude a short shaft segment at the crossing; the visible inner and outer shaft segments remain collinear.
Reconstruct tidy original gunwale wood/ochre-wrap pixels underneath removed malformed oars, remove all leftover bent stubs, preserve lashings for the fixed bronze spears.

Everything else in Image 1 stays invariant: the single narrow oak hull, four crosswise rowing benches, slatted bow fighting platform, two bronze-tipped spare spears, ochre midships wraps, source size and source framing, bow up, perfectly vertical orthographic overhead camera and warm upper-left light.
